Valence Electrons and the Octet Rule: Valence electrons are the outermost electrons and determine bonding; for main-group elements the group number gives the count. The octet rule says atoms gain, lose or share electrons to reach 8 valence electrons, like a noble gas (hydrogen and helium follow the duet rule of 2). Metals lose electrons to form cations and nonmetals gain electrons to form anions. Electrons in an ion equal atomic number minus charge. Exceptions include boron compounds with 6 electrons and period 3 or lower elements with expanded octets.
Ionic Bonds and Compounds: An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, usually formed when a metal transfers electrons to a nonmetal. Ionic compounds form crystal lattices described by formula units, with total positive charge equal to total negative charge; the criss-cross method gives formulas such as Al2O3. They have high melting points, are brittle, and conduct electricity only when molten or dissolved. Lattice energy increases with higher ion charges and smaller ions, so MgO melts higher than NaCl.
Covalent Bonds and Lewis Structures: A covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons between nonmetal atoms, forming molecules. Single, double and triple bonds share 1, 2 and 3 pairs, and more shared pairs mean shorter, stronger bonds. To draw a Lewis structure, count total valence electrons (adjusting for charge), connect atoms with the least electronegative atom in the center, complete octets with lone pairs, and use multiple bonds if needed. Formal charge equals valence electrons minus nonbonding electrons minus bonds. Resonance describes several valid structures for one species.
Molecular Shapes and Polarity: VSEPR theory says electron pairs around a central atom repel and spread as far apart as possible. Two groups give a linear shape, three trigonal planar, four tetrahedral (109.5 degrees); a lone pair gives trigonal pyramidal (NH3) or bent (H2O). Electronegativity differences classify bonds: below 0.4 nonpolar, 0.4 to 1.7 polar covalent, above 1.7 ionic. A molecule is polar only if it has polar bonds arranged asymmetrically so the dipoles do not cancel, which is why CCl4 is nonpolar but NH3 is polar.
Metallic Bonds and Intermolecular Forces: In metallic bonding, delocalized valence electrons form a sea around positive metal ions, explaining conductivity, malleability, ductility and luster. Alloys such as brass, steel and bronze mix a metal with other elements. Intermolecular forces attract separate molecules and are weaker than bonds: London dispersion forces act in all substances and grow with molecular size, dipole-dipole forces act between polar molecules, and hydrogen bonds occur when H is bonded to N, O or F. Stronger forces give higher boiling points, as in water compared with H2S.
